output.headline: Sánchez pledges to rebuild confidence in Spain's high-speed rail network
output.bodyHtml:
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has declared three days of mourning and pledged to strengthen safety on the country's high-speed rail network, after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured when one high-speed train rear-ended another, which officials suggested was caused by an “inexplicable” error at the central command centre.

The crash turned the municipality of Urda, surrounded by olive groves and vineyards, into a hub for the rescue effort. A local sports centre became a triage centre for those with minor injuries, while a nearby hall was repurposed into a space for those scrambling to find their missing loved ones.

A constant flow of vehicles from local, regional and national emergency services headed in and out of the town, while locals pitched in by bringing food and bottles of water to those waiting anxiously for news of their relatives.

The trains, one from Spain's state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.

The tragedy was the second major deadly high-speed train accident this year in Spain, rattling a country where the extensive rail network has long been a point of pride. “Today all of Spain is grieving,” Sánchez said.

In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía. On Wednesday Sánchez said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.

The Urda crash, which ranks as one of Europe's deadliest such disasters this century, comes weeks before general elections in which Sánchez is waging an uphill battle for re-election. The crash in January left his Socialist party fending off criticisms that it had not done enough to maintain the safety of the high-speed rail line, suggesting that this latest crash would add to the fractious political climate.

Images from the scene showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the rail line. Officials said the trains had been carrying 544 people.

Spain's transport minister, Óscar Puente, said that rear-end collisions like that which had taken place on Wednesday were “highly unlikely” and suggested that the accident may have been caused by human error made in “inexplicable” circumstances.

He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time due to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of around 63km of track, he said.

The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. Minutes after the computer malfunction, the centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place, said Puente.

“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”

The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said on Wednesday afternoon that the death toll had risen to 68 as rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage of the derailed carriages. Castilla-La Mancha's leader, Emiliano García-Page, told reporters that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

Officials said another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.

Miguel, a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident to Cope radio. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” he said. “Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one.”

Giving initial details about the crash, Puente said the Iryo train had been travelling ahead on the tracks and had been sitting stationary when the Renfe train was instructed by the command centre to resume its journey. The Renfe train then travelled approximately 25km before colliding with the Iryo train about 17 minutes later.

The speed at which the Renfe train had been travelling remains unknown, the transport minister told reporters, though the section of rail on which it was travelling allows for speeds of up to 200km/hour.

The control centre “had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it”, Puente added. “I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts.”

Puente said that similar erroneous instructions had been given to at least one other train on Wednesday morning. “And it was the engineer of one of the trains who corrected the command centre and told them he can't resume normal operation – it has to be [an] on-sight operation,” Puente said, citing a protocol that allows trains to advance but at a greatly reduced speed in order to ensure that there are not other trains sitting on the tracks ahead. “The operator said: ‘OK, on-sight operation.’”

Amid growing anger over the crash, the prime minister said there was little to suggest that the two high speed rail collisions Spain has suffered this year had shared any kind of similar cause.

“Everything strongly suggests that the causes of the two accidents are completely unrelated, but it is not up to me to say so,” he said. “But what is clear is that, if we need – as we certainly do – to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, it will be done.”

Across the country, people held moments of silence for those who were killed, while Spain's football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.

The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People's party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The opposition People's party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain's entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.

Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report
output.standfirst: Spain's prime minister has pledged a full investigation and promises to strengthen rail safety, after a high-speed train rear-ended another near Toledo, killing at least 68 people in the country's second fatal high-speed rail crash this year.
output.progress: Sánchez has promised a full investigation and says safety on the high-speed network will be strengthened to rebuild public confidence.

output.headline: Tommy Robinson found guilty of harassing two journalists
output.bodyHtml:
Robinson was found guilty on both counts against him on Wednesday at Southwark crown court. The jury had deliberated for two days and had to be directed by the judge that they could return a majority verdict rather than a unanimous one.

After he was found guilty, the Crown Prosecution Service said Robinson had “weaponised social media”. Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS's special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Nobody should be made to fear violence because of the work they do. Journalists play an important role in a democratic society and should be able to carry out their professional duties without being subjected to harassment.

“We will always seek to work with the police to prosecute those who break the law and I hope these convictions provide reassurance that such behaviour will be treated seriously by the criminal justice system.”

Welcoming the verdict, a spokesperson for the Daily Mail said: “Yaxley-Lennon's behaviour was reprehensible, and had grave consequences for our reporters and their families. Through his actions, Yaxley-Lennon sought to undermine our right to hold him to account. We stand by our journalists and their freedom to report legitimately in the public interest.”

Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.

Journalists from the Daily Mail and their family members fled their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, his trial was told.

Robinson had shared pictures of the family of one of the journalists online and said he had “tagged and bagged” all three reporters who worked on an article about his alleged role influencing unrest that broke out after the 2024 Southport murders. The charges related to two of the journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after an alleged campaign of intimidation that also included a call to the editor of the Daily Mail in which Robinson said he would make the journalists and their families “famous”.

Journalists were given an escort out of the courtroom by security after one of them was threatened inside the court by one of Robinson's supporters. The man was ejected from the press gallery and later from the courtroom.

Robinson, a former member of the British National party and co-founder of the English Defence League, had said before the trial that his legal bills were being paid for by the billionaire tech mogul and owner of X, Elon Musk.

He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence through posts shared with his hundreds of thousands of followers on X and by direct messages. He called Young on 5 August 2024 and told him that he would visit his house, saying: “I'm coming to get you.”

Robinson, who attended court each day with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail tracked him down to a hotel in Cyprus, where he was commenting on events in the UK after the Southport murders, and published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.

Dirnhuber said in a witness statement he did not know how Robinson had obtained his address, or who he had shared it with, adding: “I was concerned about the risk of being intercepted on my way to work, either by Robinson for a livestreamed interview or by an unpredictable supporter of his hoping to cause me or my partner physical harm.”

Young said he felt his family was under threat and he was fearful of what might happen next. “It was clear to me that Tommy Robinson was following through on his threats. My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me, or my home, or my family for what I had written.”

A third Daily Mail journalist, George Odling, said in a witness statement that he, his wife and young child had to leave their home through a neighbour's house because they feared being followed by Robinson's supporters.

The trial heard that Robinson's “angry” and “retaliatory” posts began on 5 August 2024, as he questioned the Daily Mail's decision to photograph and write the story about him in Cyprus.

In a post on X, which has been viewed 244,000 times and made reference to the newspaper's front page headline “Stoking riots from his sunbed”, he wrote: “Quick question, these lies have a direct result on threats to my family.

“Is it ok if I track down the journalists addresses + families details + dox them. Would that be journalism. This has been coordinated from the top down because my latest documentary humiliates their lies.

“They have purposely doxxed where my children are is it fair for me to do the same to them.”

Robinson said in evidence he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified the hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk. He said he had only wanted to question the journalists and claimed they knew he was “not coming to beat them up”.

Robinson is due back in court on 16 December for a sentencing hearing. Mr Justice Cavanagh said after the verdict he would be considering all options, including a custodial sentence, whether in full or suspended. Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
output.standfirst: A jury at Southwark crown court found Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing two journalists who had to flee their homes after what the trial heard were 'bullyboy, intimidatory tactics'; he faces up to 10 years in prison.
output.progress: The Crown Prosecution Service says the convictions show that harassing journalists will be treated seriously by the justice system.

output.headline: Russell Brand gives evidence for four hours as rape and sexual assault trial continues
output.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand has told a court that he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women.

The 51-year-old comedian said he had “misused” his position “very selfishly” and dedicated his life to “reckless philandering and idiocy”.

But he insisted that “consent is more important than sex itself” and that the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Mr Justice Bennathan told jurors they should find Brand not guilty of the indecent assault allegation after he concluded “there was insufficient evidence” to support the charge.

Brand is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Wearing a dark suit, white shirt and tie, he appeared in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday as he gave evidence at Southwark crown court.

He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after marrying the US pop star Katy Perry in 2010 but that now nobody would “touch him with a bargepole”.

He blamed his downfall on “devastating” 2023 media reports about his alleged sexual misconduct, which he said had led to him being barred from visiting his baby son when he was having open heart surgery at Great Ormond Street hospital.

He also said he had failed to persuade a single person with relevant information to give evidence on his behalf at his criminal trial. “Would they touch you with a bargepole?” his barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked. Brand replied: “No.”

The TV personality gave confident answers in a booming voice to Winter, issuing a series of terse “no” replies when asked if he had raped women in a hotel room, at his home and in a bar toilet, and sexually assaulted radio and TV workers.

He told the court he was “innocent” of all the charges and said: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself.”

He later added: “Consent is an ongoing process and at any point anybody can withdraw their consent.”

During the course of his evidence, Brand told the court he does not remember some of the incidents in the charges and remembers only consensual sexual encounters in others.

He admitted saving the telephone number of a woman who accuses him of anal rape in 2009 with the letter “T” next to her name, meaning “tart”.

The woman alleges Brand raped her at his north London townhouse, a few days after she had willingly engaged in a threesome with the star backstage at the Hammersmith Apollo venue in London.

When Winter asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.”

He also put two asterisks next to the woman's name, which he told the jury meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”

Brand used colourful language to describe some of his accusers. He described a woman who alleges he raped her at the Labour party conference in 1999 as “vivacious and loquacious” and an MTV worker who accuses him of oral rape in 2004 as having “prominent eyes”. “She was lithe, elfin, pixieish, energetic,” he said.

But there were tense moments during cross-examination in which Brand stared at the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, in silence for several seconds. Occasionally he could be seen moving his lips before speaking out loud.

The prosecutor probed him about alleged inconsistencies in his previous statements and what he has told the jury with regards to the woman who accused him of anal rape. Brand said: “Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree. Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection.

“It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life I've focused on at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness, well, not your forgiveness.

“I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that.”

And when asked if the young fan was “just another sexual conquest” in his attempt to sleep with 5,000 women, Brand told the court: “I really don't know the number, but it's difficult to dispute that's how I conducted myself in the pursuit of willing sexual partners.”

As he came to the end of his cross-examination, Karmy-Jones challenged Brand on what he had done to upset the woman so much. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.

“You were in a position of power in respect of each of these women,” the prosecutor continued, to which Brand replied: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong.”

Karmy-Jones also confronted him with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, in which Brand said he “would never have relented until I received my birthright orgasm”. Responding to one of the passages, Brand said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

“With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy.”

The prosecutor said that Brand's book included a picture of himself as a seven-year-old with the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took fifteen years to produce results.”

The first alleged rape victim has told the court she believed Brand was gay when they first met at a Labour party conference fringe event, which led to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.

The prosecutor asked Brand: “That's something you would do, wasn't it? That was something you would do to make girls trust you?”

“No,” Brand replied.

The trial continues.
output.standfirst: The former comedian, facing seven charges of rape and sexual assault against six women, denies all wrongdoing but told the court he was wrong to use his fame to 'facilitate' sexual access, saying consent is 'more important than sex itself'.
output.progress: The judge has already directed jurors to find Brand not guilty of one charge, after concluding there was insufficient evidence to support it.

output.headline: Palestinian parties make historic gains as both main Israeli blocs fall short of majority
output.bodyHtml:
Israel's future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday's elections.

Turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting. Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot's bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu's coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister's bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots – about 14% of the total electorate – yet to be fully counted.

With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

On Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and the success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming they had “stolen the election”. He did not offer evidence, but said on X that his Likud party had sent “hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence” to the central elections committee and the Shin Bet internal security agency.

Both those agencies have been politicised under Netanyahu's government. The elections committee had sought to ban Arab Israeli parties before the poll, but the attempt to exclude them was overturned by the country's supreme court.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu's better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot's Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra'am (the United Arab List).

“We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu's racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.

Related: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel's political landscape

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can't be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu's government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to their rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other's camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

The Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.

On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.

“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.

The election happened in the midst of Israel's war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

A UN commission of human rights experts reported on Monday that Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.

The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Israel's ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel's ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.

Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.

The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel's southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war alongside the US against Iran.
output.standfirst: Record turnout and a historic surge in support for Palestinian parties left both Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition and Gadi Eisenkot's opposition short of the 61 seats needed for a majority, with coalition talks and more vote-counting still to come.
output.progress: Yair Golan is urging the opposition to negotiate a coalition with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra'am, rather than freeze them out.

output.headline: EU and Canada press ahead with plans for 'ever closer association'
output.bodyHtml:
The EU and Canada will press ahead with plans for “an ever closer association”, after the EU backed away from its initial offer to start talks on Canada becoming an “associate member”, following disagreements between member states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month's state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.

The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.

It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.

Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen's declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.

Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen's] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU's proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada's largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.

Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.

Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.

“The good news is it doesn't matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”

A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.
output.standfirst: A planned Canada-EU summit in Montreal will instead work towards 'an ever closer association' after the EU's unprecedented offer of 'associate membership' for Canada ran into pushback from member states including Germany and Italy.
output.progress: Carney says the label matters less than 'the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians', as formal negotiations continue towards next year's summit.

output.headline: Prosecutor praises 'extraordinary bravery' of passengers who fought off LNER knifeman
output.bodyHtml:
Passengers fought back against a knifeman who, a court heard, “caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale” when he stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train.

Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on an LNER train on 1 November last year and stabbing four people in the 24 hours before.

The prosecutor also praised the “extraordinary bravery” of the passengers who tried to wrestle the knife off Williams.

This included Scott Green, who was stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was also stabbed multiple times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.

Paxton also praised the train driver for his decision to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon.

Christopher Paxton KC told jurors at Cambridge crown court on Wednesday: “The defendant, Mr Williams, armed with a knife, caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale, moving up and down a busy train from which there was no escape, stabbing several people as he did so.”

During his opening statement, Paxton showed a CCTV clip of a passenger, Stephen Crean, attempting to wrestle a knife from Williams. He said Williams asked Crean: “Do you want to die?”

“We say, clear evidence of the defendant's intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many, and to stab and cut Mr Crean in his hand, head and lower back,” Paxton said.

Paxton described the “terror” of the attack, which led some train passengers to run “for their lives” and hide away in toilets, store cabinets and under seats.

Williams, of no fixed abode, previously admitted a series of offences, including the wounding of 12 people, but denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

Paxton told the court Williams posed a “dangerous threat” to the people he encountered before the train attack on the evening of 1 November.

Jurors heard Williams had approached a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November and asked him if he was “beefing the devil” before he knifed him in the face and hand.

Williams also attacked three people in Peterborough on the evening of 31 October, the court heard, including a 14-year-old boy.

“Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered, the defendant, Anthony Williams, posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife,” he said.

“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear.”

The trial continues on Thursday.
output.standfirst: Anthony Williams, accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on a London-bound train, denies the charges; several passengers and a crew member were stabbed as they tried to disarm him, and the driver made an emergency stop.
output.progress: The train driver made an emergency stop and several passengers and a crew member fought to disarm Williams, suffering stab wounds themselves.

output.headline: UK and Netherlands pledge major new aid for Ukraine as Starlink service is restored
output.bodyHtml:
Britain is to provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems – as the country heads into what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet of the war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after speaking to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government's annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You've made my day’.”

The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.

The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine's utilities and manufacturing.

Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine's president announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk's genius and said he was in touch with Starlink's controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.

The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk's SpaceX with Russia's gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.

“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we're only taking the first steps.”

The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.

A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.

Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.

Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire's leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine's war effort.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other's way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.

Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.

“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they'll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.

Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.

Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.
output.standfirst: Britain pledges £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over three years, plus an immediate £500m for air defences, as the Netherlands adds further aid – while Vladimir Putin praises Elon Musk's 'genius' and Russia builds a satellite network of its own to use against Ukraine.
output.progress: Britain and the Netherlands are stepping up funding for Ukraine's air defences and reconstruction, and Starlink and Starshield speeds have been restored to normal.

output.headline: Media groups say duty to sources and public compels them to publish misconduct claims
output.bodyHtml:
Two news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.

The anonymous individual, known in court simply as PPT, is seeking an injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies.

His legal team have argued that publishing would be likely to lead to his death, after two previous attempts to take his own life.

However, the legal team for the media groups told the high court there were powerful “countervailing” considerations compelling them to publish the claims.

Gavin Millar KC, the lead barrister for the media outlets, said they had “not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest”.

He argued the claimant had not taken the impact on the sources involved in the investigation “sufficiently into account”.

“They have made a substantial commitment to being contributors, and were extremely anxious for the publication and the broadcast to go ahead as soon as possible,” Millar said.

Many of the women making the allegations have been traumatised by PPT's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result, according to a written submission from the media groups.

It states: “They believe that it is important that their allegations are publicly aired so that other women are protected and the full nature of his conduct is disclosed, and in order to assist the sources to recover from their own experiences.”

It said the media outlets had credible evidence of seriously improper conduct “towards a large number of women over a prolonged period”, including potential criminal conduct.

Millar said if publication of the allegations were blocked, “our women contributors and others we are aware of” were likely to find “other ways to make their stories known publicly”.

He added that proceeding with publication through the Guardian and ITN would be the “best way to put the information into the public domain”.

The well-known figure is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

However, the media companies argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never ruled in such a way that would cause these articles to apply in this case. They also argue countervailing rights under article 10, which protects the right to freedom of expression.

Millar said the investigation into PPT had spoken to more than 100 people, including 30 who gave first-hand accounts.

He told that court that since the Guardian and ITN first contacted PPT in May so he could respond to the allegations, deadlines had been repeatedly extended and unusual measures put in place in order to act responsibly, given PPT's medical issues.

Millar said that “recognising the difficult and unusual nature of the case”, the media companies had then agreed to delay publication so that PPT could seek an injunction and have his case heard before a judge.

PPT's legal team has previously told that court there was evidence his life would be endangered should the allegations be published.

A summary of an assessment of the claimant's current wellbeing by an independent expert stated that he could not conclude either that suicide was inevitable if publication went ahead, or that psychiatric treatment could eliminate all risk.

The expert said that the risks could be lowered should the allegations be published while PPT was in an inpatient psychiatric setting.

The trial has now concluded, with Mr Justice Nicklin retiring to come to a ruling.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
output.standfirst: The Guardian and ITN told the high court they have a duty to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by an anonymous public figure, known as PPT, who is seeking a permanent injunction, citing a high risk of suicide.
output.progress: The outlets say they repeatedly extended deadlines and took unusual steps to act responsibly towards PPT's health while preparing to publish allegations from more than 100 people.

output.headline: Telegraph's new owner presses on with plans to build a 'leading centre-right' global outlet
output.bodyHtml:
The controversial Daily Telegraph columnist Allison Pearson is understood to be in negotiations about leaving the broadsheet as the newspaper's new owner makes significant newsroom cuts.

Sources told the Guardian that Pearson – firmly on the right of the Telegraph's roster – is preparing to announce her exit imminently and is crafting a statement about her future plans.

Related: Telegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as new owner promises to turn paper into ‘AI-powered’ global business

The news comes after the German media company Axel Springer, which completed a £575m takeover in June, warned that as many as 100 journalists' roles were at risk of redundancy as it transitioned into being “a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.

When the Telegraph's purchase was announced – ending three years of uncertainty over its future – Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer's chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he planned to invest in the title as he wanted to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.

The Telegraph will also focus on increasing its audience globally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, according to an email to staff from the chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol.

She added: “To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”

One insider said the Brexit-backing columnist had been “in some sort of negotiation to make an elegant departure” after discussions with management about her future at the title.

But they said rumours of her expected exit had been circulating within the newsroom for a number of days, and were not a surprise after a column she wrote in September had raised some eyebrows internally, particularly among senior management.

Pearson wrote in an opinion piece that the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had “the rough-diamond charisma to pull a large, enthusiastic crowd”.

She also wrote: “Every single person who marched in the rain to Unite the Kingdom, every decent person hanging our beautiful flags from lamp-posts and motorway bridges and on village greens, is making patriotism respectable again. Step by step, inch by inch, we are taking our country back from those who hate it.”

Pearson has been the Telegraph's chief interviewer and a columnist since 2010. But her relations with some senior editorial figures were said to be strained over a number of subjects she raised in her columns, particularly around immigration.

Other managers did not welcome the attention she brought to the title when she was investigated by police in Essex in 2024 for allegedly stirring up racial hatred with a social media post.

The force was criticised by Pearson and her supporters when officers knocked on her door on Remembrance Sunday over a photograph she retweeted amid heightened tensions over the policing of Gaza protests. Pearson deleted the post and the police investigation was dropped, but a review concluded the force was right to look into the allegations.

Some staff at the Telegraph said that in the difficult period since the cuts were announced, the newsroom had felt like “a morgue”.

Proposed changes include folding separate departments such as health and travel into one features department.

A spokesperson for the Telegraph declined to comment, saying they could not discuss the employment status of individual staff members.

Pearson has been approached for comment.
output.standfirst: Axel Springer, which completed a £575m takeover of the Telegraph in June, is reorganising the newsroom to expand globally, as the columnist Allison Pearson is reported to be negotiating her exit amid the job cuts that are part of the overhaul.
output.progress: Axel Springer says it is restructuring the paper for clearer accountability and faster decision-making as it invests in global expansion.
